source.title: Catastrophic Fisher Explosion: Early Phase Fisher Matrix Impacts Generalization
source.authors: Stanislaw Jastrzebski; Devansh Arpit; Oliver Åstrand; Giancarlo Kerg; Huan Wang; Caiming Xiong; R. Socher; Kyunghyun Cho; Krzysztof J. Geras

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests noisy-label learning and memorization with Fisher-penalty interventions, rather than testing the original fully randomized-label fitting setup.
record.gate_note: The study changes 25% or 50% of CIFAR-100 training labels to uniform random labels and reports test accuracy and clean/noisy training accuracy. It does not test fully random labels, unstructured inputs, training time across corruption levels, or the effects of weight decay, dropout, or augmentation on random-label fitting.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures clean versus noisy training accuracy and learning trajectories under partial label corruption. Baseline results bear on V4, and Figures 5 and 11 bear on V6. Improvements from the proposed regularizers alone do not establish either version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate if the mechanism remains a hypothesis: FP slows learning of incorrect labels more than clean labels, and the authors hypothesize that this strengthens SGD's existing bias toward learning clean examples first. FP also slows clean-example learning.
record.recipe_differences: Studies partial uniform label corruption on CIFAR-100 and intervenes with Fisher Penalty and comparator regularizers; it does not reproduce the original fully random-label fitting experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with label-noise fraction (25% versus 50%), model, and regularization method. The authors describe different impacts for clean and noisy examples under Fisher Penalty.

fits_no_version.finding: FP, GPr, and mixup improve best-validation-selected test accuracy under partial label noise; GPx results vary by model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: These regularizers can improve generalization with uniformly corrupted CIFAR-100 labels.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; proceedings of the 38th ICML, PMLR 139 (2021)
record.problems: Only vision tasks are studied. The noisy-label experiment tests 25% and 50% corruption, not a full corruption sweep or fully random labels. The text does not report uncertainty for Table 3 or Tables 8–9. Table 3 labels a model ResNet-52, while the setup describes Wide ResNet and VGG-11.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported noisy-label results within the 60-row limit were left out.

untested.parts: Completely random training labels, unchanged hyperparameters relative to true-label training, and chance test performance.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Training fit on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian inputs.
The complete zero-to-total-corruption sweep, chance endpoint, and perfect training fit at 50% corruption.
Controlled tests of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation preventing random-label fitting, and their removal affecting true-label generalization.
Wholly random-label datasets and generalization beyond the tested CIFAR-100 architectures and training settings.

missing.what: Clean and noisy training-accuracy trajectories across FP coefficients, including baseline and matched-clean-accuracy comparisons; these directly measure differential learning dynamics absent from the endpoint rows.

record.verdict_notes: All judgments use the supplied text. ResNet naming is inconsistent: tables say ResNet-52, Figure 11 says ResNet-50, Section 4.1 says ResNet-32, and experimental details specify Wide ResNet. Missing experimental coverage is untested, not a scope limitation. V6 does not promise cost-free clean learning, so FP's clean-learning cost does not itself limit V6.

versions.untested_parts: Whether standard networks fit a completely random labeling with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters, and the associated chance test error.
Training-time cost and convergence speed across label-corruption fractions.
The full sweep from no corruption to all labels random, perfect training fit at every fraction, and a steady rise in test error across that sweep.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation prevent random-label fitting or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
The claim for wholly random labels and unmodified standard training; the reported comparison uses 25% or 50% corrupted labels and Fisher-penalty or other regularization conditions.
